Part V - Graphical client¶

The interface is a client of the core. It imports neither the physics nor the learning part and does not use PyTorch: everything it shows arrives as frames (Section 1), and everything it does is a command of the protocol (Part IV). Sections 1-3 need no display (frame model, tiles, marks); Section 4 draws them; Section 5 connects Qt to the core; Sections 6-9 are the panels; Section 10 is the controller that translates between panels and commands; Sections 11 and 12 compose the window and start it.

Part V, Section 1: what the interface knows about the model.

Theory¶

The interface owns no model. Everything it shows is a frame: the dictionary and the arrays of one frame event (Part IV, Section 1). This module turns a frame into a read-only object, FrameModel, and derives from it what the plots need - which atoms are shown, a common histogram of their intensities, the atoms that lie inside the mask. None of this needs Qt, so it is tested without a display.

Visible atoms. An atom of layer \(l\) is shown if its occupancy \(o = \sigma(\vartheta)\) is at least the display threshold \(o_{\min}\) and its intensity is finite. The threshold is a property of the view; the model is never changed by it.

Histogram. The intensities \(I_i\) of all visible atoms of all layers are binned into \(B = 101\) bins that span the finite range of all layers together, so that the curves of different layers can be compared.

Loss history. The core sends one light event per optimiser step. The history keeps at most HISTORY_LIMIT values; when the limit is reached every second point is dropped and the sampling stride doubles, so that a run of millions of steps stays cheap to draw.

Part V, Section 2: the tiles of the plot area.

Theory¶

The plot area is a grid of tiles; every tile shows one quantity. The set and order of the tiles follows from the model alone:

loss  sim  diff  target  ctf | pot0 ... pot(L-1) | hist  ux  uy  eps_xx  eps_yy  eps_xy

(ctf is the probe in STEM; L is the number of layers). While seeding the displacement field is not trained, so the five strain tiles are left out.

Three views exist: all tiles in a grid of five columns; one tile large with the loss curve beside it; and the comparison sim | target | diff with a common zoom and the loss underneath. plan() turns a view into rows, columns and the positions of the tiles, so that the canvas only has to draw.

Part V, Section 3: marks drawn over the images.

Theory¶

Three kinds of marks lie over the images: the atoms, the gradient arrows and the candidate sites. What is drawn depends on the zoom, so the numbers are computed here, without Qt, and the canvas only draws them.

Marker size. A marker of fixed size becomes dust when one zooms in and a colour smear when one zooms out. The area is therefore

\[s = \mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{1200}{\Delta},\; 0.5,\; 60\right)\ \mathrm{pt^2}, \qquad \Delta = \max(\text{width},\,\text{height})\ \text{of the visible window [px]}. \tag{3.1}\]

Gradient arrows. For an atom with position \(\mathbf r_i\) and gradient \(\mathbf g_i = \partial L/\partial \mathbf r_i\), the arrow points along \(-\mathbf g_i\) (the direction of descent; optionally \(+\mathbf g_i\)) and has the length

\[\ell_i = \ell_{\max}\,\frac{|\mathbf g_i|}{g_{\rm ref}}, \tag{3.2}\]

where \(g_{\rm ref}\) is the largest \(|\mathbf g|\) of all atoms (lengths stay comparable while zooming) or, on request, of the atoms in the visible window. Only arrows inside the window are drawn, and at most MAX_ARROWS of them (those with the largest \(|\mathbf g|\)).

Part V, Section 4: the plot canvas.

Theory¶

PlotCanvas draws a FrameModel into the tiles of Section 2. It follows three rules.

  • Artists live as long as the layout. A new frame only replaces the data of existing artists, so the zoom (toolbar, mouse wheel) survives updates. A layout is built again only when the view, the seeding flag or the model changes.

  • The loss curve is cheap. A light event redraws only the axes of the loss (blitting); drawing 15 panels of megapixel images would cost over a second.

  • Marks follow the zoom. Marker sizes and arrows (Section 3) are recomputed 30 ms after the view stopped changing.

Part V, Section 5: the connection to the core.

Theory¶

The interface talks to the core through temsim.service.client.Client, which delivers events in its transport thread and blocks while a command is answered. Qt wants neither: widgets may only be touched from the GUI thread, and the GUI thread must not wait for a simulation. Connection bridges the two.

Events arrive in the transport thread, are converted (a frame event becomes a FrameModel) and re-emitted as Qt signals; Qt queues a signal that is emitted from another thread, so the slots run in the GUI thread.

Commands are submitted to a single worker thread, in order, and their result is handed back by a signal. Because there is one worker, the order in which the user pressed buttons is the order in which the core sees the commands - the guarantee of Part IV, Section 1. Connection.submit() takes the callable that performs the call, a done callback for the result and an failed callback for a RemoteError.

Starting a core. spawn_core() runs python -m temsim.service serve as a child process on a free local port and waits until it answers; the interface then owns the process and ends it on exit. Data is opened by a command afterwards, never by the command line, so that the model has one owner only (Part IV, Section 2).

Part V, Section 6: small building blocks of the panels.

Theory¶

None of the panels needs more than a handful of widget kinds: a spin box with a range, a section that can be folded away, and a box with a form inside. They are made here once, so that the panels read as a list of what is shown, not how.

Part V, Section 7: the numbers that are edited by hand.

Theory¶

A reconstruction has a few dozen numbers that a person may want to set directly: the amplitude contrast, the energy spread, \(C_c\), the aberration coefficients, the two normalisation constants of the image, and for every group its shift, rotation, scale and contrast. The core publishes exactly these under flat keys (temsim.service.session.Session.values()), always as magnitude and angle for the aberrations, whatever it uses internally.

ValuesEditor builds one spin box per component from the dictionary it is given, so that new groups or aberrations appear without a change here, and writes a changed key back with set_values. The values keep changing while the optimiser runs, so ValuesEditor.refresh() shows new numbers; a spin box that has the focus is left alone, so that typing is never overwritten.

Part V, Section 8: what is trained, and how it is weighted.

Theory¶

The optimiser of Part II is steered by TrainSettings: for every trainable quantity a switch and a learning rate, the weights of the loss terms (Part II, Section 1) and of the priors (Section 3), the flags that select single aberrations and envelope terms, and the active group - the group whose mask and target count and which, if the group asks for it, is simulated alone.

TrainEditor shows these settings and changes them. It keeps a copy of the settings, built from the experiment and the settings that it is given, and sends every change as the smallest command that expresses it:

  • a switch or learning rate -> set_param,

  • a loss or prior weight -> set_loss / set_regularisation,

  • the active group -> set_active_group,

  • the flag dictionaries and the two presets, which change many things at once -> set_train without the bulk arrays (the core keeps its masks and targets).

Two presets are common enough to have buttons. TrainEditor.train_only_group() freezes everything except the rigid transformation (shift, rotation, scale) of one group, makes that group active and keeps the optics free unless the group is simulated in isolation - without the rest of the structure the optics cannot be determined. TrainEditor.free_positions_training() freezes everything except the positions of the individual atoms of all layers.

Part V, Section 9: the control panels.

Theory¶

The right-hand column of the window consists of four panels. A panel is only a set of widgets: it knows its defaults, how to show a state and how to hand its settings out, but nothing about the core; the Controller connects panels, canvas and connection. This is what makes the panels testable without a core and keeps the interface replaceable: a new button needs a widget here and one line there.

  • ControlPanel - state, training buttons, view options, resets, gradient arrows, removal of weak atoms.

  • MinimaPanel - candidate sites from the minima of the difference image (Part II, Section 5) and the checks that a candidate has to pass.

  • SeedingPanel - the options of the random seeding; the numbers are those of SeedConfig plus the three job options.

  • StrainPanel - the number of control points of the displacement field of every group.

Part V, Section 10: the controller.

Theory¶

The interface is a client: it holds no model and computes nothing. What a person does - pressing a button, moving a spin box - becomes a command to the core; what the core reports - a status, a light or a frame event - becomes a change of the panels and the canvas. Controller is the one place where this translation happens, so that the panels (Section 9) stay free of the protocol and the connection (Section 5) stays free of the panels.

Who changes what. The core is the only owner of the state. The controller never assumes that a command had an effect: after every edit it asks for a new frame (render) and shows that. The only state kept here is view state - the zoom, the display threshold of the occupancy, the loss history - and the memory of what was last done, which decides two conveniences of the old interface:

  • after a seeding, the first start of training releases the positions and intensities of the seeded atoms (unless the person has chosen the trainable quantities);

  • the seeding view leaves out the strain tiles, because the displacement field is not trained while seeding.

Candidate sites. While the optimiser runs, the core would have to build a seeder to test the sites, which costs time that belongs to the optimisation. Candidates are therefore requested without the loss test while a job runs (yellow marks) and with it when the core is idle or paused (green marks), as in the old interface.

Part V, Section 11: the main window.

Theory¶

The window is a composition and nothing else: the plot area on the left, a scrollable column of panels on the right, the editors below. The proportions are those of the old interface (splitter 4:1, window 1600 x 950). All behaviour lives in Controller.

Part V, Section 12: starting the interface.

The interface connects to a running core (--endpoint) or starts one of its own. Data is opened by a command after the connection, never by the core’s command line (Part IV, Section 2).
